t: Reply calmly to an angry customer in minutes
d: Paste in a heated complaint and get a warm, firm reply that acknowledges the problem, explains what happens next and keeps the customer.
when: Whenever a complaint makes your heart race

steps.h: Copy the complaint, minus personal details
steps.b: Copy the customer's message and replace their name, order number and address with placeholders like [Customer] before you paste it anywhere.

steps.h: Note the facts on your side
steps.b: Jot down in a line or two what actually happened and what you can offer, such as a refund, replacement or call back.

steps.h: Ask your AI assistant for a draft
steps.b: Open ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini and paste this prompt with the complaint and your notes.
steps.p: You are helping a small business reply to an upset customer. Here is their message: [paste complaint]. Here are the facts from our side: [what happened]. What we can offer: [refund / replacement / discount / call back]. Write a reply under 150 words that: 1) opens by acknowledging how they feel without grovelling, 2) takes responsibility for anything we got wrong, 3) explains clearly what we will do and by when, 4) ends with one easy next step for them. Tone: warm, calm, human, British English. Do not promise anything not listed in our offer. Then give me a shorter 2-sentence version for text or WhatsApp.

steps.h: Read it as the customer would
steps.b: Check every promise is something you can keep, add their name back in, and send it from your usual inbox.

example: Hi [Customer], I'm really sorry your order arrived damaged, just before the weekend. That's not the standard we aim for. I've sent a replacement today by tracked delivery, so it should be with you by Thursday. If you'd prefer a full refund instead, just reply 'refund' and I'll sort it straight away.
tips: If you are still annoyed, wait ten minutes before sending, even with a good draft.
Ask for two versions, one more formal and one more casual, and pick what fits your brand.

trigger.detail: An email arrives with words like complaint, refund or disappointed

actions.detail: Rate how upset the customer is and what they are asking for
Draft a calm reply using the business's agreed offers
Save the reply as a draft for the owner to check

t: Build a ready-to-use FAQ from your old emails
d: Turn the questions customers keep asking into a tidy FAQ document with clear answers you can paste into emails, your website or chats.
when: Once, then refresh every few months

steps.b: Search your inbox for words like 'how do I', 'when will' and 'can I' and copy the questions into one document. Remove names, emails and order numbers as you go.
Under each question, add a rough note of what you usually say, even if it's messy. Include prices, delivery times and policies as they are today.

steps.h: Ask your AI assistant to organise it
steps.b: Paste your notes into ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini with this prompt.
steps.p: Here is a list of questions my customers ask and my rough answers: [paste]. My business: [one line about what you sell or do]. Turn this into a customer FAQ. 1) Merge duplicate questions. 2) Group them under 4 to 7 headings (for example Orders, Delivery, Payments, Returns). 3) Write each answer in plain British English, under 60 words, friendly and specific. 4) Keep all facts exactly as I gave them and mark anything unclear with [CHECK]. 5) At the end, list 5 questions customers probably ask that are missing from my list.

steps.b: Fix every [CHECK] item, then save the FAQ in Google Docs where your whole team can find it. Pin a link in your bookmarks.

example:
Delivery
How long does delivery take? Most orders arrive in 2 to 4 working days. You'll get a tracking link by email as soon as it ships.
Returns
Can I return a sale item? Yes, within 14 days, as long as it's unused. [CHECK: do personalised items count?]
tips: Date the document and update it whenever a price or policy changes, so nobody gives out old answers.
The 'missing questions' list is great material for your website's help page.

trigger.detail: Every three months

actions.detail: Remind the owner to gather new customer questions
Merge new questions into the FAQ and flag anything out of date
Save the refreshed FAQ as a new dated version

t: Get an AI helper that drafts replies from your policies
d: Set up a private AI workspace that knows your FAQ and policies, so every reply draft uses your real prices, rules and tone.
when: Every time you answer a customer question

steps.b: Collect your FAQ, returns policy, delivery info and price list into one or two documents. Make sure none of them contain customer details.

steps.h: Create a workspace in your AI assistant
steps.b: Use a Project in ChatGPT or Claude, or a Gem in Gemini, depending on what your plan includes. Upload your documents as its files or knowledge.
Paste this into the workspace's instructions box so it behaves the same way every time.
steps.p: You help me reply to customers of [business name], which [what you do]. Always answer using only the uploaded documents. If the answer isn't in them, say 'I don't know from your documents' and suggest what I should check. Write in British English, warm and short (under 120 words), using the customer's first name if I give it. Never invent prices, dates or policies. After each draft, list in one line any facts you used and which document they came from.

steps.h: Use it for each new question
steps.b: Paste the customer's question with personal details removed and ask for a reply. Check the facts line before you copy the draft into your email or chat.
When a policy or price changes, replace the old file in the workspace straight away.

example: Hi Sam, yes, you can swap the size for free within 30 days. Just pop it back in the original bag with the returns slip, and we'll send the new size as soon as it arrives. Facts used: free exchanges within 30 days (Returns policy, section 2).
tips: Check your workplace AI policy before uploading business documents.
Keep the AI as your drafting helper, not a bot talking to customers directly, until you've tested it for a few weeks.

trigger.detail: A new customer question arrives

actions.detail: Draft a reply using only the business's uploaded policies
Show the draft and the facts used for a person to approve

t: Set up friendly WhatsApp Business auto-replies
d: Write a welcome message, an out-of-hours away message and a set of quick replies so WhatsApp customers always get a helpful first response.
when: Once, then update when your hours or offers change

steps.h: List what people message you about
steps.b: Scroll through recent WhatsApp chats and note the 5 to 8 questions that come up most, such as opening hours, prices, booking and delivery.

steps.h: Ask your AI assistant to write the messages
steps.b: Paste this prompt into ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini.
steps.p: I run [business type] and use WhatsApp Business. My opening hours: [hours]. Common questions: [list]. Write: 1) a greeting message for first-time chatters (under 40 words), 2) an away message for outside hours that says when I'll reply and where to find urgent info (under 40 words), 3) a quick reply for each common question (under 50 words each), with a short shortcut word for each, like /hours or /prices. Tone: friendly, local, British English. Use [brackets] where I need to add details.

steps.b: In the WhatsApp Business app, open Business tools and set up the Greeting message, Away message and Quick replies. Paste each message and its shortcut.
Ask a friend to message you, then try typing / in a chat to check your quick replies appear.

example: Away message: Thanks for your message! We're closed right now but will reply by 10am tomorrow. Opening times and prices are on our catalogue. /booking: You can book a slot here [link]. Pick any time that suits and you'll get a confirmation straight away.
tips: These features are in the free WhatsApp Business app, not regular WhatsApp, so switch if you're using your personal account for work.
Keep the away message honest about reply times; a promise you keep beats a fast one you miss.

trigger.detail: Owner updates hours or offers

actions.detail: Rewrite greeting, away and quick reply messages with the new details
Remind the owner to paste them into WhatsApp Business

t: Sort your support inbox into labels automatically
d: Gmail filters that file incoming customer emails into Refunds, Delivery, Bugs and Other, so you can deal with the urgent ones first.
when: Runs every time an email arrives

steps.b: Pick 4 to 6 labels that match the work, for example Refunds, Delivery, Technical, Sales and Other. Create them in Gmail from the left sidebar.
Paste a handful of real subject lines (no names or addresses) and this prompt into your AI assistant.
steps.p: I want Gmail filters that sort customer emails into these labels: [list labels]. Here are example subject lines and first sentences from each type: [paste examples]. For each label, give me a list of 8 to 12 words or short phrases to put in a Gmail filter's 'Has the words' box, joined with OR, in a format I can paste straight in. Avoid words so common they'd catch everything. Then list any emails from my examples that might be caught by two filters, and suggest which should win.

steps.h: Create a filter for each label
steps.b: In Gmail, click the search options icon in the search bar, paste one keyword list into 'Has the words', then choose Create filter and tick Apply the label. Repeat for each category.
Look at what lands in each label daily. Move anything misfiled and add its words to the right filter in Gmail's settings, under Filters.

example:
Refunds: refund OR "money back" OR chargeback OR "return my" OR cancel OR overcharged
Delivery: tracking OR courier OR "not arrived" OR "where is my" OR delayed OR dispatch
tips: Don't tick 'Skip the inbox' at first; keep everything visible until you trust the filters.
Outlook users can do the same with Rules, found in Outlook's settings under Mail.

trigger.detail: Any new email to the support address

actions.detail: Decide whether it is a refund, delivery, technical, sales or other request
Apply the matching label
Alert the owner if it looks urgent

t: Solve customer problems from their photos and screenshots
d: Upload a customer's photo or screenshot and get a plain-English read of what's wrong plus a step-by-step reply to help them fix it.
when: When a customer sends a picture instead of an explanation

steps.h: Check the image for private details
steps.b: Crop out or blur names, addresses, card numbers and faces before uploading. Most phones have a markup or crop tool in the photo editor.
Attach the image in ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini and paste this prompt.
steps.p: A customer sent this image with the message: [paste their message]. Our product/service: [what it is]. 1) Describe what you can see that's relevant to the problem. 2) Give the 2 or 3 most likely causes, most likely first. 3) Write a friendly reply with numbered steps they can follow to fix it, under 120 words, British English. 4) Tell me what to ask them if the steps don't work. If you can't tell from the image, say so rather than guessing.

steps.b: You know your product best, so remove any step that doesn't apply before sending the reply.

example: What I can see: the error 'Payment declined: address mismatch' on the checkout page. Likely cause: billing postcode differs from the card's. Reply: Hi Jo, thanks for the screenshot! 1) Check the billing postcode matches your card statement. 2) Try again. If it still fails, reply and we'll send a payment link.
tips: Screenshots of error messages work best; ask customers for one when they say 'it won't work'.
Save good replies into your FAQ so you don't need AI next time.

trigger.detail: A customer message arrives with an image attached

actions.detail: Read the error or problem shown in the image
Draft step-by-step fix instructions
Show the draft for approval before replying

t: Save ten perfect replies to your most common questions
d: A set of polished Gmail templates you can drop into any email in two clicks, written once with AI and reused for months.
when: Set up once, use every day

steps.b: In Gmail's settings, look in the Advanced tab for Templates and switch them on, then save changes.
Write down the ten things you answer most often, plus the key facts for each.

steps.h: Write them all in one go
steps.b: Paste your list into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: Write 10 email reply templates for [business name], a [type of business]. For each, give: a short template name, a subject line, and a body under 100 words. Questions and facts: [paste list]. Style: warm, clear, British English, sign off as [your name]. Start each with 'Hi [Name],' and use [square brackets] for anything I'll fill in each time, such as order numbers or dates. End each with one clear next step.

steps.b: Open a new email, paste one reply, then use the three-dot menu at the bottom of the compose window and choose Templates, then Save draft as template. Name it to match.
When replying, insert a template from the same menu, fill in the brackets and add one personal line at the top.

example:
Template: Delivery delay
Hi [Name],
Thanks for checking in. Your order [number] is with the courier and running about [X] days behind. Here's your tracking link: [link]. If it hasn't arrived by [date], reply to this email and I'll send a replacement.
Best, Priya
tips: Always add one line that's specific to the customer so it never feels canned.
In Outlook, use My Templates or Quick Parts for the same thing.

trigger.detail: A customer asks a common question

actions.detail: Match the question to one of the saved templates
Create a reply from the template with blanks filled where known

t: Spot the problems your customers complain about most
d: A simple complaints log in a spreadsheet plus a monthly AI review that shows your top issues, trends and the fixes worth making first.
when: Log as you go, review on the first Monday of each month

steps.b: Make a sheet with columns: Date, Channel, Category, What went wrong, What we did, Resolved (Yes/No). Add a dropdown for Category using Data validation in the Data menu.
Add one row per complaint in a sentence. Leave out names, emails and order numbers so the sheet stays safe to share.
Create a recurring Google Calendar event on the first Monday of each month called 'Complaints review'.

steps.h: Ask AI to find the patterns
steps.b: Copy the last month's rows and paste them into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: Here is my customer complaints log for [month]: [paste rows]. Columns: Date, Channel, Category, What went wrong, What we did, Resolved. Please: 1) give a table of complaint types with counts, most common first, 2) say what changed compared to last month: [paste last month's top 3 or 'first month'], 3) pick the 3 problems where one fix would prevent the most complaints, and suggest a practical, low-cost fix for each, 4) flag any complaint left unresolved for more than 7 days. Keep it under 300 words.

steps.b: Choose one change to make this month and note it at the top of the sheet so you can see if complaints drop.

example: Top issues in March: Late delivery (11), Wrong size sent (6), Website checkout error (4). Change: late delivery up from 5. Best fix: add a dispatch-date note on product pages during busy weeks. Unresolved over 7 days: 2 (rows 14, 22).
tips: Excel works just as well; use a drop-down list for Category so the counts stay tidy.
Share the one-paragraph summary with your team; it's often the push needed to fix a long-running issue.

trigger.detail: First Monday of each month at 9am

actions.detail: Count and rank complaint types from the log
Suggest the three most valuable fixes
Save the monthly complaints review
Send the summary to the owner

t: Reply to every online review in your own voice
d: Thoughtful, personal responses to good and bad Google reviews in minutes, so potential customers see you care.
when: Once a week, or when a new review arrives

steps.b: Open your Google Business Profile (search your business name on Google while signed in) and copy any reviews you haven't answered yet.
Paste the reviews into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: I own [business name], a [type of business] in [town]. Write a public reply to each review below. Reviews: [paste, one per line with star rating]. Rules: under 70 words each; mention one specific thing the reviewer said; thank them by first name only if they used one; for 1 to 3 stars, apologise for their experience without arguing, mention one thing we're doing about it ([what you're changing]), and invite them to contact [email or phone] to put it right; never reveal any private details about the customer; British English; vary the wording so replies don't all sound the same.

steps.b: Read each reply aloud, make sure nothing confirms private details like what treatment or service someone had, then post it on the review.

example: 5 stars: Thanks so much, Leah! We're thrilled the cinnamon buns made your Saturday. See you next time. 2 stars: We're sorry the wait was so long on Sunday. We've added a second person on the till at weekends. Please email hello@[cafe].co.uk so we can make it up to you.
tips: Reply to bad reviews within a couple of days; a calm public reply often matters more to readers than the review itself.
For health, legal or financial services, never confirm someone was a client in a public reply.

trigger.detail: Every Friday at 3pm

actions.detail: Collect new unanswered reviews
Draft a personal reply for each review
Send drafts to the owner to approve and post

t: Tell customers clearly when something goes wrong
d: A calm, honest message to all affected customers about a delay, outage or mistake, with versions for email, social media and your website.
when: When a problem affects many customers at once

steps.b: Note what happened, who is affected, what you're doing about it, and when you'll next update people. Stick to what you know for sure.
Paste your notes into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: Something has gone wrong at [business name]. Facts: [what happened]. Who is affected: [customers]. What we're doing: [actions]. When customers will hear from us next: [time]. Anything we're offering: [refund / credit / nothing yet]. Write: 1) a customer email (subject line plus under 150 words), 2) a social media post under 280 characters, 3) a two-sentence banner for our website. Be honest and specific, apologise once, do not speculate about causes we haven't confirmed, and avoid jargon. British English.

steps.h: Send it and keep your promise
steps.b: Send the email through Mailchimp or your usual email tool, post the update, and set a reminder for the time you said you'd update people next.

example:
Subject: Your order is running a few days late
Hi there, our courier had a warehouse fault on Monday, so orders placed between 3 and 5 May will arrive 2 to 3 days later than planned. We're really sorry. Every affected order now has free delivery refunded, and we'll email you a fresh tracking link by Friday.
tips: Send a short follow-up when it's fixed; customers remember that more than the problem.
If the issue involves people's personal data, speak to a professional adviser before you send anything, as there may be legal steps to follow.

trigger.detail: Owner reports an incident

actions.detail: Write email, social post and website banner versions
Prepare the customer email for review
Add a reminder for the promised follow-up update

t: Turn support requests into an organised to-do list
d: A simple online help form that drops every request into a spreadsheet with a status column, plus email alerts when a new one arrives.
when: Runs every time someone submits the form

steps.b: Ask your AI assistant to suggest the questions so you get what you need first time.
steps.p: I'm making a customer support request form for [business type]. Suggest 5 to 7 questions that would let me solve most problems without emailing back. For each: the exact question wording, the best answer type (short answer, paragraph, dropdown, multiple choice, file upload) and dropdown options where relevant. Include a question on urgency. Keep it quick to fill in on a phone, and only ask for personal details I truly need.

steps.b: Create a new form, add the questions, and add one line at the top saying how you'll use their details and how fast you reply.

steps.h: Link it to a sheet and turn on alerts
steps.b: In the form's Responses tab, link it to a new Google Sheet. In the same tab's menu, turn on email notifications for new responses.
In the sheet, add columns for Status (New, In progress, Done) and Owner, using a dropdown. Use Format, then Conditional formatting, to colour urgent requests red.
Put the form link in your email signature, website contact page and WhatsApp away message.

example: Row 23: 14/05 10:12 | Order issue | Urgency: High | 'Parcel says delivered but not here' | Status: New | Owner: Tom. Row 24: 14/05 11:40 | Product question | Low | 'Is the large bag waterproof?' | Status: Done | Owner: Ana.
tips: Microsoft Forms and Excel can do the same if your business uses Microsoft 365.
Only share the sheet with people who need it, because it holds customers' contact details.

trigger.detail: A customer submits the support form

actions.detail: Add the request as a new row with status New
Set urgency and category
Email the team about urgent requests

t: Run a simple ticket board from your support inbox
d: Customer emails turn into cards on a Trello board automatically, get a checklist and due date, and move across columns as you work on them.
when: Runs whenever a support email arrives

steps.b: Create a Trello board with lists: New, Waiting on customer, In progress, Done. In the board's menu, find the Email-to-board settings and copy the board's email address, choosing the New list.

steps.h: Forward support emails to the board
steps.b: In Gmail's settings, add the Trello address under Forwarding. The confirmation code will appear as a card on your board. Then create a filter for your support emails and choose Forward to that address.
Open the board's Automation menu and add rules, for example: when a card is added to New, set it due in 1 day and add your checklist; when a card moves to Done, mark it complete.
Ask your AI assistant for a consistent handling checklist to use in your rule.
steps.p: Write a 5 to 7 step checklist for handling a customer support request at [business type], from first reading to closing. Each step under 8 words, starting with a verb. Include checking the FAQ, replying within [24 hours], confirming the fix with the customer and logging the issue type. Then write a one-line rule for when a ticket should move to 'Waiting on customer'.

steps.b: Each morning, drag cards along as you deal with them and reply from Gmail as normal. Check the forward filter hasn't missed any emails for the first week.

example: Card: 'Re: Broken handle on order 4471' | Due tomorrow | Checklist: Read and tag issue / Check FAQ / Reply within 24h / Arrange replacement / Confirm it's fixed / Log issue type. Moved to Waiting on customer: 2 cards. Done this week: 17.
tips: Trello's free plan limits automation runs, so check usage if you get lots of emails.
Cards hold copies of customer emails, so keep the board private to your team.

trigger.detail: A support email matches the forwarding filter

actions.detail: Create a card in the New list
Tag the card by issue type and urgency
Suggest a first reply to attach to the card

t: Answer customers in their own language
d: Understand a message in any language and send back a natural, accurate reply in that language, with an English copy for your records.
when: When a message arrives in a language you don't speak

steps.b: Copy the customer's message into ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, removing any account numbers or addresses.

steps.h: Ask for a translation and reply
steps.b: Use this prompt so you understand the message and get a reply in one go.
steps.p: Here is a customer message: [paste]. 1) Tell me what language it's in and translate it into English. 2) Point out anything that might be lost in translation, like tone or slang. 3) Here is my reply in English: [your reply]. Translate it into the customer's language so it sounds natural and polite for a small business, not word-for-word. 4) Translate your version back into English so I can check the meaning is unchanged.

steps.b: Read the English back-translation. If the meaning has shifted, ask the AI to fix that sentence before you send.

example: Language: Polish. Translation: 'Hello, I ordered two jars but received one. Can you send the second one?' Tone: polite, a little disappointed. Your reply in Polish: 'Dzień dobry, bardzo przepraszamy za pomyłkę...' Back-translation: 'Hello, we're very sorry for the mistake. The second jar ships today.'
tips: For refunds, contracts or anything legal, mention that the English version is the official one.
Add a line saying you used translation, so customers forgive the odd awkward phrase.

trigger.detail: A customer message in another language arrives

actions.detail: Translate the message into English
Translate the approved reply into the customer's language
Show both versions to the person replying

t: Start each day with a summary of overnight messages
d: A five-minute morning routine that summarises new customer emails, ranks what's urgent and suggests who should handle each one.
when: Every working morning

steps.b: Make sure customer emails get a label such as Support, using a Gmail filter on your support address or common words.
Add a recurring 15-minute Google Calendar event each working morning called 'Overnight support check'.

steps.h: Use built-in AI if you have it
steps.b: If your plan includes Gemini in Gmail, open the Support label, open the Gemini side panel and ask it to summarise unread emails in this label. Otherwise copy the emails into your AI assistant.
Use this prompt with whichever AI you're using.
steps.p: Here are customer emails received since [time yesterday]: [paste, or refer to the unread emails in my Support label]. Give me a table with: sender first name, one-line summary, category, urgency (High/Medium/Low) and suggested owner from this team: [names and what they handle]. Put High urgency first. Mark High if the customer is waiting on a delivery today, has been charged wrongly, or is threatening to leave. Then list any that could be answered with a standard reply.

steps.b: Share the table in your team chat or just work down it yourself, starting at the top.

example: High: Ellie - charged twice for order - Billing - Owner: Sam. High: Dev - wedding cake order for Saturday, no confirmation - Orders - Owner: Mia. Medium: Kofi - asks about gluten-free options - Product - Owner: Mia. Standard reply possible: 3 delivery-time questions.
tips: Copilot in Outlook can do the same summary if your plan includes it.
Check your workplace AI policy before pasting customer emails into an AI assistant.

trigger.detail: Every weekday at 8:30am

actions.detail: Summarise unread Support emails from overnight
Rank by urgency and suggest an owner
Post the ranked list to the team chat

t: Hand over a customer case without losing anything
d: Turn a long, messy email or chat thread into a short handover note so a colleague can pick up the case without rereading everything.
when: Before holidays, shift changes or passing a case on

steps.b: Open the email or chat thread and copy it all, oldest message first if possible. Replace bank details and passwords with [removed].
Paste the thread into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: Turn this customer support thread into a handover note for a colleague. Thread: [paste]. Use these headings: Customer and issue (2 lines), What's been tried, What we've promised and by when, Customer's mood and preferences, Open questions, Next step (one clear action). Keep it under 200 words. Quote any exact promise word-for-word. If dates or amounts conflict in the thread, flag them.

steps.b: Post the note in Slack, Teams or email to your colleague, along with a link to the original thread.

example: Customer and issue: Amira, kitchen tap leaking after install on 2 June. Tried: washer replaced 9 June, still dripping. Promised: 'a plumber visit before Friday 16th'. Mood: patient but tired of chasing; prefers text. Open: is the tap under warranty? Next step: book plumber and text Amira a time today.
tips: The 'promises' heading is the most valuable; broken promises are what turn a case into a complaint.
Keep handover notes in the same place each time, like a pinned Slack thread or shared doc.

trigger.detail: Agent marks a case for handover

actions.detail: Summarise the thread into a structured handover note
Send the note to the colleague taking over

t: Turn a recorded walkthrough into a customer help guide
d: Record yourself explaining a fix on Zoom, then turn the transcript into a clear step-by-step help article customers can follow alone.
when: When you keep explaining the same thing over and over

steps.b: Start a Zoom meeting on your own, share your screen and talk through the task as if a customer were watching. Turn on recording with an audio transcript if your plan includes it.
Download the transcript from your Zoom recordings once it's ready. On a free plan, use your phone's voice recorder app with transcription, or type rough notes as you go.
Paste the transcript into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: Here is a transcript of me explaining how to [task] for customers of [product/service]: [paste]. Turn it into a help article. Include: a clear title, a one-sentence 'what you'll need', numbered steps (one action each, under 25 words), a note where a screenshot would help written as [Screenshot: what it shows], a 'If it doesn't work' section with 3 common fixes, and a short summary at the top. Remove filler words and anything I said that was a mistake. British English, friendly, no jargon.

steps.b: Paste the guide into Google Docs, add the screenshots where marked, and share the link or copy it to your website's help page.

example:
How to reset your booking password
You'll need: the email you booked with.
1. Go to the booking page and tap 'Log in'.
2. Tap 'Forgotten password'. [Screenshot: login screen]
3. Check your inbox for an email from us...
If it doesn't work: check spam, use the original email, or contact us.
tips: Walk through the guide yourself on a phone before sharing; it shows any missed step fast.
Make sure no customer details are visible on screen while recording.

trigger.detail: A new recording transcript appears in the help-guides folder

actions.detail: Turn the transcript into a step-by-step help article
Create a draft guide document with screenshot markers
Let the owner know the draft is ready to check

t: Find out how customers felt after you helped them
d: A two-question satisfaction survey sent after each solved case, low scores highlighted automatically, and a monthly AI summary of what people say.
when: After every solved case, with a monthly review

steps.b: In Google Forms, ask 'How happy are you with the help you got?' on a 1 to 5 scale and 'What could we do better?' as a paragraph. Make the second question optional.

steps.h: Link it to a sheet and highlight low scores
steps.b: Link responses to a Google Sheet. Use Format, then Conditional formatting, to turn rows red when the score is 2 or less, and turn on form email notifications so you hear about them straight away.

steps.h: Add the link to a closing template
steps.b: Write a short 'glad we could help' Gmail template with the form link and use it whenever you close a case.
Set a monthly calendar reminder, then paste that month's responses (no names) into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: Here are this month's customer satisfaction responses (score 1 to 5, comment): [paste]. 1) Give the average score and how many responses. 2) Group comments into themes with counts. 3) Quote the 3 most useful comments word-for-word. 4) Suggest 2 practical changes based on low scores. 5) Write a one-paragraph summary I can share with my team. Don't infer anything that isn't in the comments.

steps.h: Close the loop on low scores
steps.b: Contact anyone who scored 1 or 2 within a couple of days, if they left contact details, to put things right.

example: October: average 4.4 from 38 responses. Themes: quick replies (14), friendly staff (9), had to repeat information (6), slow refunds (4). Change ideas: add order number to form; confirm refund date in every refund email. Low scores to follow up: 3.
tips: Ask for contact details only if they want a follow-up, and say so on the form.
Microsoft Forms and Excel can be used the same way, including email alerts for new responses.

trigger.detail: A customer submits the satisfaction survey

actions.detail: Add the score and comment to the results sheet

t: Walk into every sales call fully prepared
d: A one-page brief on a prospect's business, recent news, likely needs and smart questions to ask, ready in five minutes before the call.
when: Before every sales call

steps.b: Note the company's website, the person's job title and anything they told you when they booked. A quick look at their LinkedIn company page helps too.

steps.h: Ask your AI assistant for a brief
steps.b: Use an assistant that can search the web, such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini with search turned on, and paste this prompt.
steps.p: I have a sales call with [name, job title] at [company], website [URL]. I sell [what you sell] to [type of customer]. Search the web and give me a one-page brief: 1) what the company does in 2 lines, 2) size and location if public, 3) any news from the last 6 months, 4) 3 problems they likely have that I could help with, and why you think so, 5) 5 open questions to ask on the call, 6) one thing to avoid saying. Include the source link for every fact and say clearly if you couldn't find something.

steps.b: Click two or three of the source links to confirm the key facts, especially news and numbers.
Paste the brief into your notes app or the calendar event so it's open when the call starts.

example: Greenway Joinery: bespoke kitchens, about 25 staff, two showrooms in Leeds. News: opened a second showroom in March (source). Likely needs: more enquiries from new area; quicker quoting. Ask: 'How are leads from the new showroom tracking?' Avoid: assuming they sell online.
tips: AI can mix up companies with similar names, so always check the website matches.
Only use information that's publicly available, and don't dig into anyone's personal life.

trigger.detail: One hour before a meeting tagged 'sales'

actions.detail: Look up the prospect's company website and recent news
Write a one-page brief with questions to ask
Send the brief to the user before the call

t: Write a cold email that people actually answer
d: A short, personal first email to a potential client that leads with their problem, not your sales pitch, plus two subject lines to test.
when: Before contacting a new prospect

steps.h: Find one real reason to write
steps.b: Look for something specific about the prospect: a new branch, a job advert, a post they wrote, or a review. That's your opening line.
Paste this prompt into your AI assistant.
steps.p: Write a cold email from me, [your name], [what you do], to [their job title] at [company]. Reason I'm writing: [the specific thing you noticed]. The problem I think they have: [problem]. Proof I can help: [one result for a similar client, no names]. Rules: under 110 words; first line about them, not me; one clear, low-effort ask such as a 15-minute call or 'shall I send an example?'; no buzzwords, no flattery, no fake urgency; British English; plain text. Give me 2 subject lines under 6 words each and one alternative opening line.

steps.b: Read it out loud and change anything you wouldn't say in person. Add a line letting them know how to say no thanks.

steps.h: Send it from your own inbox
steps.b: Send it one at a time from Gmail or Outlook, not as a bulk blast, and note the date in your lead list.

example:
Subject: Your new Leeds showroom
Hi Jess, congrats on the Leeds opening. New showrooms often get lots of browsers but slow quote requests. I helped a Sheffield kitchen fitter double their booked consultations in three months with a simple follow-up routine. Would a 15-minute call next week be useful? No worries if not.
tips: Rules on business emails differ by country; in the UK and EU you need a fair reason to contact someone and an easy way to opt out.
Send fewer, better emails; ten researched ones beat a hundred generic ones.

actions.detail: Write a personalised cold email from the prospect notes
Save it as a draft for the user to check and send
Mark the prospect as 'Draft ready'

t: Build a list of local businesses to approach
d: A tidy spreadsheet of local businesses in your target area, gathered from Google Maps and cleaned up by AI, ready for careful outreach.
when: When you want new local clients

steps.h: Search Google Maps for your ideal customer
steps.b: Search for a business type in an area, such as 'dog groomers in Bristol'. Open each result and note the name, website, phone, rating and anything that shows they need you.

steps.h: Paste your rough notes into a sheet
steps.b: Don't worry about tidiness; paste names, links and notes into a Google Sheet as you go. Aim for 20 to 40 businesses.

steps.h: Ask AI to clean and sort it
steps.b: Copy the rough rows into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: Here are rough notes on local businesses I might sell to: [paste]. I offer [what you sell]. Turn this into a table with columns: Business name, Website, Phone, Google rating, Number of reviews, Fit score (1 to 5), Reason for score, Opening idea. Score higher if [signs they need you, e.g. no website, low review count, outdated photos]. Remove duplicates, keep my facts exactly as written, and put 'unknown' rather than guessing missing details. Sort by Fit score, highest first.

steps.h: Paste the table back into your sheet
steps.b: Paste the AI's table into a new tab, then add columns for Contacted (date) and Outcome.
Start with the best-fit businesses, using their public business contact details and a personal message.

example: 1. Paws & Bubbles | pawsbubbles.co.uk | 0117 xxx | 4.8 (12 reviews) | Fit 5 | Great reviews but no online booking | Opening idea: 'Your reviews are brilliant; shall I show how online booking could fill your quiet Tuesdays?'
tips: Collect it by hand rather than with scraping tools; it's slower but keeps you within Google's terms and gives you better notes.
Only store business contact details, and delete businesses that ask not to be contacted.

trigger.detail: User chooses a business type and area

actions.detail: Look up public business listings for the area
Score each business for fit and note why
Add the cleaned leads to the lead sheet

t: Know which leads to call first
d: Score every lead in your spreadsheet against your own simple criteria, with a short reason, so you spend time on the people most likely to buy.
when: Weekly, or when new leads pile up

steps.h: Write down what a great lead looks like
steps.b: List 4 to 6 signs of a good fit, like budget size, location, how they found you and how soon they need help. Note one or two deal-breakers too.
Copy the lead rows from your sheet, including any notes or form answers. Leave out personal phone numbers and emails, as the AI doesn't need them.
Paste the rows and your criteria into your AI assistant.
steps.p: Score these sales leads from 1 to 10 using my criteria. Good signs: [list]. Deal-breakers: [list]. Leads: [paste rows with an ID for each]. Return a table: Lead ID, Score, Hot/Warm/Cold, One-line reason, Suggested next step. Only use information in the rows; if something important is missing, lower the confidence and say what to ask. Put Hot leads first.

steps.h: Add the scores to your sheet
steps.b: Paste the Score and Reason columns back next to each lead using the IDs. Sort by score and colour Hot leads with conditional formatting.
Treat scores as a starting point. If you know something the AI doesn't, change the score.

example: L-104 | 9 | Hot | Needs a new website by March, budget £3k+, referred by a client | Call today. L-107 | 4 | Cold | Student project, no budget mentioned | Send helpful guide. L-110 | 6 | Warm | Good fit but no timeline | Ask when they want to start.
tips: Look back after a month: did Hot leads really buy? Adjust your criteria if not.
If your plan includes Gemini in Google Sheets, you can ask it in the side panel instead of copying rows out.

trigger.detail: A new lead is added to the sheet

actions.detail: Score the lead against the user's criteria
Write score, rating and reason into the row
Alert the user about Hot leads

t: Follow up politely when prospects go quiet
d: Three short, friendly follow-up emails, each adding something useful, scheduled to send on the right days from your own inbox.
when: When someone hasn't replied for a week

steps.b: Copy your last message to them and note what they were interested in. Remove anything confidential.

steps.h: Ask AI for a gentle sequence
steps.b: Paste this prompt into your AI assistant.
steps.p: I sent this to a prospect and got no reply: [paste last email]. They were interested in [topic]. Write 3 follow-up emails for days 5, 12 and 21. Each under 70 words, in British English, warm and not pushy. Email 1: friendly nudge plus one useful tip. Email 2: share a short example or result relevant to them. Email 3: a polite 'shall I close your file?' that makes it easy to say not now. No guilt-tripping, no 'just checking in'. Reply in the same thread so give no new subject lines.

steps.b: In Gmail, reply in the same thread, paste the first follow-up, and use the arrow next to Send to choose Schedule send. Add calendar reminders for the next two, since you'll stop if they reply.
If they reply at any point, cancel the remaining reminders and answer them personally.

example: Day 5: Hi Ben, a quick thought on the menu reprint: printing seasonal specials on a separate card often saves reprinting the whole menu. Happy to show a sample. Day 21: I don't want to fill your inbox, so shall I close this for now? If timing's better in spring, just say and I'll check back then.
tips: Outlook also has a schedule send option under the Send button's arrow.
The third email often gets the most replies, because it's easy to answer.

trigger.detail: Daily check for prospects with no reply after 5 days

actions.detail: Write the next follow-up in the sequence
Place it as a reply draft in the same thread
Remind the user to review and send

t: Reply to new enquiries before your competitors do
d: Website or social enquiries land in a sheet, you get an instant alert, and a ready-made personal reply is waiting to send.
when: Every time someone fills in your enquiry form

steps.b: Create a Google Form asking for name, email, what they need, budget range, timing and how they found you. Add a line on how you'll use their details.

steps.h: Send responses to a sheet and turn on alerts
steps.b: In the form's Responses tab, link it to a Google Sheet and switch on email notifications for new responses. On your phone, allow Gmail notifications so you see them fast.

steps.h: Write a reply template with AI
steps.b: Ask your AI assistant for a first-reply template you can personalise quickly.
steps.p: Write a first reply to a new enquiry for [business], which offers [services]. Use [brackets] for their name, what they asked for and timing. It should: thank them, show I've read their request with one specific line, give one helpful piece of information about [price range / process], and offer two ways forward (a 15-minute call via [booking link] or a reply with more details). Under 120 words, British English, warm and professional. Also write a 40-word version for WhatsApp or text.

steps.h: Save it as a Gmail template
steps.b: Turn on Templates in Gmail's settings under Advanced, then save the reply as a template so you can insert it in one click.

steps.h: Aim to reply within the hour
steps.b: When an alert arrives, open the sheet, insert your template, fill in the brackets and send.

example: Hi Hannah, thanks for getting in touch about a garden redesign for your back patio this spring. Most patio projects like yours start from £2,500, depending on materials. Easiest next step: book a free 15-minute call here [link], or reply with a couple of photos and I'll suggest some ideas.
tips: Speed matters: people often go with whoever answers first.
Keep the sheet private, since it contains people's contact details.

trigger.detail: A new enquiry form is submitted

actions.detail: Log the enquiry with date and source
Personalise the first-reply template
Create the reply draft for the user
Send a push alert about the new enquiry

t: Turn every sales call into clear next steps
d: After each call, get a summary of what the prospect needs, their concerns, agreed actions and a ready-to-send follow-up email.
when: Straight after every sales call

steps.b: Tell the prospect at the start that you'd like to take notes with an AI tool and check they're happy. If not, take handwritten notes instead.
If your plan includes Zoom AI Companion or Google Meet's 'Take notes for me', switch it on for the call. Otherwise, record a voice note of your key points right after the call.

steps.h: Turn them into a summary and email
steps.b: Paste the transcript, AI notes or your voice note text into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: Here are notes from a sales call with [prospect role] at [company]: [paste]. Give me: 1) Their situation in 3 lines, 2) Needs and goals, 3) Concerns or objections, word-for-word where possible, 4) Budget and timing if mentioned, 5) Agreed next steps with who and when, 6) My honest read of how likely they are to buy and why. Then write a follow-up email under 150 words that thanks them, recaps what we agreed in bullet points and confirms the next step. British English.

steps.b: Send the follow-up the same day and paste the summary into your lead sheet or CRM notes.

example: Needs: shopfront signage before July opening. Concern: 'last sign company was months late'. Budget: around £1,800. Next steps: I send 3 design ideas by Fri; they confirm sizes by Wed. Likelihood: high, firm deadline and budget. Email: 'Thanks for your time today, Raj. As agreed...'
tips: Always check AI meeting notes for names and numbers before sending them to a client.
Store notes on prospects securely and delete them if the deal doesn't go ahead and you no longer need them.

actions.detail: Summarise needs, concerns and agreed actions from the notes
Draft a follow-up email to the prospect
Add the summary to the lead's row

t: Turn call notes into a polished proposal
d: A clear, client-focused proposal with scope, timeline, prices and next steps, built from your rough notes in about fifteen minutes.
when: After a client asks 'can you send me something?'

steps.b: Gather your notes about what the client wants, plus your prices, timescales and any terms you always include.

steps.h: Ask AI to draft the proposal
steps.b: Paste everything into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: Write a proposal from [my business] to [client company] using these notes: [paste notes]. My prices and packages: [paste]. Structure: 1) Your goals (in the client's own words where possible), 2) What I'll do (bullet points), 3) What's not included, 4) Timeline with milestones, 5) Investment (a table with 2 or 3 options, recommended one marked), 6) Why me (2 short points), 7) Next steps to get started. Plain British English, confident but not salesy, under 600 words. Use only my prices; don't invent any numbers. Mark anything you're unsure of with [CHECK].

steps.b: Paste it into Google Docs or Word, add your logo, check every figure and [CHECK] note, then export it as a PDF.

steps.h: Send with a short personal note
steps.b: Email it with two lines recapping the main benefit and suggesting a time to talk it through.

example:
Investment
Option A: Essentials - 5-page website, 3 weeks - £1,950
Option B (recommended): Essentials plus online booking and 2 months of support - £2,600
Not included: copywriting for blog posts, paid advertising.
Next steps: sign below and pay a 30% deposit to book a May start.
tips: Offering three options usually works better than a single price.
Have contract terms and payment conditions checked by a qualified professional once, then reuse them.

actions.detail: Draft a proposal from call notes and price list
Create the proposal document
Remind the user to check prices and send

t: Get confident answers to tricky sales objections
d: Practise handling 'it's too expensive' and other common pushback with an AI role-play partner, and leave with a cheat sheet of honest answers.
when: Before an important pitch, or whenever you feel rusty

steps.b: Write down the five things people say when they don't buy, such as price, timing, 'we already have someone' or 'I need to think about it'.
Paste this prompt into your AI assistant.
steps.p: I sell [product/service] to [type of customer] at around [price]. Common objections I hear: [list]. For each, give me: what the person might really mean, one question to understand it better, and a short, honest reply (under 50 words) in a natural, non-pushy British tone. Never suggest pressure tactics or misleading claims. Then put it all in a one-page table I can keep beside me.

steps.b: In the same chat, ask: 'Now play a sceptical [job title] at a [business type]. Push back with my objections one at a time and wait for my reply. After 5 exchanges, tell me what I did well and what to improve.' Type or use voice mode to answer.
Copy the cheat sheet and your best answers into your notes app for your next call.

example: 'It's too expensive.' Might mean: unsure of the value, or comparing to a cheaper quote. Ask: 'What are you comparing it with?' Reply: 'That's fair. The difference is that ours includes aftercare for a year, so there are no surprise call-out fees. Would it help if I broke down the cost?'
tips: Voice mode in ChatGPT or Gemini makes the role-play feel much closer to a real call.
If you hear the same objection a lot, it may be telling you something about your offer, not your pitch.

trigger.detail: User starts a practice session

actions.detail: Write an objection cheat sheet for the user's offer
Role-play a sceptical buyer and give feedback
Save the cheat sheet

t: Find out why your sales page isn't converting
d: An honest review of your landing page with the top problems, a rewritten headline and clear fixes, ranked by how much difference they'll make.
when: When visits are coming in but enquiries aren't

steps.b: Take full screenshots of your page on a computer and on your phone, or copy all of its text. Note who the page is for and what you want visitors to do.
Attach the screenshots or paste the text into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: Review my sales page as if you were a busy [ideal customer]. The goal is for visitors to [book a call / buy / sign up]. Here it is: [attach screenshots or paste text]. Give me: 1) what you understand I offer after 5 seconds, 2) the 5 biggest problems stopping people taking action, ranked by impact, each with a specific fix, 3) 3 alternative headlines that say the benefit clearly, 4) any missing trust signals (reviews, guarantees, prices, photos), 5) one thing that already works well. Be direct and specific. British English.

steps.b: Fix the two highest-impact issues first, then wait a couple of weeks to see if enquiries change before doing more.

example: 5-second read: 'Some kind of wellness service?' Top problem: headline 'Holistic solutions for you' doesn't say what you do. Fix: 'Sports massage in Cardiff for runners and cyclists'. Problem 2: booking button only at the bottom. Fix: add it under the headline. Works well: genuine client photos.
tips: Ask a real customer the same 5-second question; if their answer matches the AI's, you know it's right.
Change one thing at a time so you can tell what made the difference.

trigger.detail: User submits a page link

actions.detail: Read the page content
List ranked problems, fixes and new headlines
Save the review as a checklist

t: Start genuine conversations with prospects on LinkedIn
d: Personal connection notes and a short message plan for your best prospects, tracked in a simple Notion list so nobody slips through.
when: A few times a week, 15 minutes at a time

steps.b: In Notion, create a database with columns: Name, Company, Profile link, Why them, Status (To connect, Connected, Talking, Not now) and Next step date.

steps.h: Pick five people at a time
steps.b: Choose prospects who post or comment regularly. Note one thing from their recent posts or profile in the Why them column.
Paste your notes into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: I help [type of customer] with [what you do]. For each person below, write: 1) a LinkedIn connection note under 250 characters that mentions the specific thing I noticed and has no sales pitch, 2) a first message to send a few days after they accept, under 60 words, that offers something useful (an idea, an article, a question about their work), and 3) a natural second message for a week later. People: [name, role, what I noticed]. British English, friendly, no flattery, no 'I'd love to pick your brain'.

steps.b: Copy each note into LinkedIn yourself and update the Status in Notion. Don't use tools that automate LinkedIn, as LinkedIn's rules don't allow them.
Open a Notion view filtered to today's next-step dates each time you sit down to do LinkedIn.

example: Connection note: 'Hi Amara, your post on running a café with two kids under five really struck a chord. Would be good to connect.' Message 1 (after accepting): 'Thanks for connecting! You mentioned staffing rotas eat your Sundays; here's a free template one of my clients uses...'
tips: Comment thoughtfully on their posts for a week before connecting; it makes the note feel natural.
Keep notes factual and work-related; your tracker should never hold anything you wouldn't be happy for them to see.

actions.detail: Write a connection note and two follow-up messages
Save the drafts and set the next-step date
