t: Keep track of every deal in a simple spreadsheet
d: A ready-made sales tracker with stages, values, follow-up dates and red alerts for overdue leads, designed with AI in an afternoon.
when: Set up once, check every morning

steps.h: Ask AI to design your tracker
steps.b: Paste this prompt into your AI assistant to plan the sheet.
steps.p: Design a simple sales pipeline tracker in Google Sheets for a [type of business] with about [number] active leads. Give me: 1) the columns in order with a one-line purpose each (include Stage, Deal value, Last contact, Next step, Next step date, Source), 2) the dropdown options for Stage, 3) step-by-step instructions to add those dropdowns and to colour rows red when Next step date is before today, written for a beginner, 4) a summary tab layout showing total value per stage, with the exact formulas to use (for example SUMIF). Keep it to what a one-person business needs.

steps.b: Follow the instructions in Google Sheets: add the columns, the Stage dropdown via Data validation, and the red overdue rule via Conditional formatting.
Enter every open conversation, even small ones, with a next step and a date.
Create a recurring 10-minute Google Calendar event each morning with the sheet's link in it, and work through anything red.

example: Stages: New, Contacted, Call booked, Proposal sent, Won, Lost. Row: Bloom Florist | Proposal sent | £1,200 | Last contact 03/06 | Next: chase proposal | 10/06 (red, overdue). Summary: Proposal sent £6,400 across 5 deals; Won this month £2,100.
tips: Write the next step as an action ('Send revised quote'), not a status ('Waiting').
Excel works the same way; ask the AI for Excel instructions instead.

trigger.detail: Every weekday at 8am

actions.detail: List overdue next steps and deals by stage
Send the user today's follow-up list

t: Create a free guide that brings in new leads
d: A short, genuinely useful checklist or guide your ideal clients will swap their email for, written with AI and designed in Canva.
when: Once, then share it for months

steps.b: Pick one specific question your clients always ask before they buy, such as 'How do I prepare my garden for a landscaper?'

steps.h: Get topic ideas and an outline
steps.b: Paste this prompt into your AI assistant.
steps.p: I'm a [your job] helping [ideal client]. Suggest 5 ideas for a free one-to-three page guide or checklist they'd happily give their email for. For each: title, the problem it solves, and why it leads naturally to hiring me. Then, for the idea I choose ([pick one or 'the best one']), write the full content: a clear title, a one-line promise, 7 to 10 practical steps or checklist items with a sentence each, one short example, and a friendly closing line inviting them to [book a call / reply]. British English, no fluff.

steps.b: Pick a guide or checklist template in Canva, paste the content in, add your logo and colours, and download it as a PDF.
Create a sign-up form in Mailchimp (or your email tool) and send the guide in the welcome email. Make it clear people are joining your mailing list.

example: Title: The 10-minute pre-survey checklist for your loft conversion. Promise: Save a second visit and get an accurate quote first time. Items: 1. Measure the highest point of the loft... 6. Photograph the water tank... Closing: Ready for your free survey? Book here.
tips: Fact-check every tip yourself; your guide is your reputation.
Only send people what they signed up for, and keep the unsubscribe link in every email.

trigger.detail: Someone signs up for the free guide

actions.detail: Send the welcome email with the guide attached
Add the new subscriber to the lead list

t: Turn bookings into warm, well-prepared sales calls
d: Prospects book through Calendly, answer a few smart questions, get reminders and a thank-you, while you get a ready brief before each call.
when: Every time someone books a sales call

steps.b: Ask your AI assistant for questions to add to your Calendly event.
steps.p: I offer [service] to [ideal client] at around [price]. Write 4 short booking questions for a free 20-minute discovery call that help me prepare and understand fit, without putting people off. Include one about their main goal, one about timing, and one about budget phrased gently with ranges. Then write: a reminder email to send 24 hours before (under 80 words) and a thank-you email to send 1 hour after the call (under 100 words) with [booking link for next step] and [resource]. British English, warm.

steps.b: Connect Calendly to your Google Calendar, then add the questions to the event's booking form so answers show in the calendar invite.

In Calendly's Workflows, if your plan includes them, add the reminder email before the event and the thank-you email after it. On a free plan, save them as Gmail templates and set yourself calendar reminders.
Before each call, copy the booking answers from the calendar event into your AI assistant and ask for 3 tailored questions and the likely best package for them.
Look at which booking answers led to sales and adjust the questions to screen better.

example: Booking answers: Goal - 'more weekday bookings'; Timing - 'next 2 months'; Budget - '£500 to £1,000'. AI prep: Ask what days are quietest now; ask what they tried before; likely fit: Starter package (£750). Reminder sent 24h before; thank-you sent 1h after with proposal link.
tips: Keep booking forms short: four questions is plenty or people drop off.
Tell people in the form that their answers help you prepare and are kept private.

trigger.detail: A new Calendly booking is added to the calendar

actions.detail: Pull goal, timing and budget from the booking answers
Write a call brief with tailored questions
Send the reminder and thank-you emails at the set times
Log the booking in the lead tracker

t: Win back old leads with a gentle email series
d: A short, automated email series that reconnects with past enquiries who never bought, offering something useful rather than pestering.
when: Set up once, then add old leads every quarter

steps.h: Gather leads who said yes to emails
steps.b: From your sheet or inbox, list past enquiries from the last year or so who agreed to hear from you. Leave out anyone who asked not to be contacted.

steps.h: Import and tag them in Mailchimp
steps.b: Import the list into Mailchimp as a CSV saved from Google Sheets, and give them a tag such as 'Old lead 2026'.
Paste this prompt into your AI assistant.
steps.p: Write a 3-email re-engagement series for people who enquired about [service] in the last year but didn't buy. My business: [one line]. What's new since then: [new offer, prices, results]. Email 1 (day 0): friendly 'thought you might find this useful' with one genuine tip. Email 2 (day 7): a short client story with a result, no names. Email 3 (day 14): a simple invitation to [book a call / special offer until date], with an easy 'not interested' link. Each under 120 words with 2 subject line options. British English, warm, no pressure.

steps.b: In Mailchimp, create an automated journey (Customer Journeys, if your plan includes it) that starts when the tag is added, then sends the three emails with waits of 7 days between them. On a free plan, schedule them as three regular campaigns to that tag.
Reply to anyone who responds yourself and move them into your sales tracker.

example: Email 1 subject: A quick tip for your spring garden. 'Hi Laura, you asked about patio cleaning last year, so here's a trick: a stiff brush and warm soapy water clears most algae before you need a pressure washer...' Results after 3 weeks: 64 sent, 31 opened, 5 replies, 2 calls booked.
tips: Only email people who agreed to hear from you; UK and EU rules on marketing emails are strict.
Remove anyone who doesn't open any of the three emails, to keep your list healthy.

trigger.detail: First day of each quarter

actions.detail: Find enquiries older than 3 months with no sale and marketing consent
Add them to the re-engagement list
Send the 3-email series on days 0, 7 and 14
Alert the user when someone replies

t: Ask happy clients for reviews and referrals
d: A warm thank-you message that asks for a review and an introduction at the right moment, with ready versions for email and WhatsApp.
when: When a client says they're pleased with your work

steps.b: Ask straight after a win: a finished project, a great result or a kind message from them.
Paste this prompt into your AI assistant.
steps.p: Write a thank-you message from me, [your name], to [client first name], whose [project] I just finished. Something specific they liked: [detail]. Ask, in a relaxed way, for: 1) a short Google review via this link [link], with 2 example prompts to make it easy (like 'what was it like working with me?'), and 2) whether they know one other [type of person/business] who might need help with [service]. Make it clear there's no pressure. Give an email version (under 120 words) and a WhatsApp version (under 50 words). British English, genuine, no sales language.

steps.b: Send from your own email or WhatsApp, and thank them again when they leave a review or make an introduction.

example: WhatsApp: Hi Sophie, thanks again for being so lovely to work with; I'm so glad the new bathroom feels calmer. If you have a minute, a quick Google review would help me loads: [link]. And if you know anyone else planning a refit, I'd be grateful for an intro. No pressure at all!
tips: Never offer payment or gifts in exchange for reviews; review sites ban it.
Keep a list of who referred whom and send a handwritten thank-you card.

trigger.detail: A project is marked Complete in the tracker

actions.detail: Write a personal thank-you with review and referral request
Draft the email for the user to send
Set a reminder to thank them after they respond

t: Decide quickly whether a tender is worth bidding for
d: A short summary of a tender or request for proposal with deadlines, requirements, scoring and a clear bid or no-bid checklist.
when: When a tender or big client brief lands in your inbox

steps.b: Save the tender documents, usually PDFs, into one Google Drive folder so nothing gets lost.

steps.h: Upload and ask for a summary
steps.b: Upload the files to ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini (or connect your Drive if your plan allows) and use this prompt.
steps.p: Summarise this tender for a small business deciding whether to bid. Give: 1) what the buyer wants in 5 bullet points, 2) all deadlines, including clarification questions, as a table, 3) must-have requirements (insurance, certifications, turnover, experience), 4) how bids are scored, with weightings, 5) the budget or contract value if stated, 6) anything unusual or risky. Then score our fit from 1 to 10 against our profile: [your size, experience, certifications, capacity] with reasons. Quote page numbers for each key point. If something isn't in the documents, say 'not stated'.

steps.h: Check the key facts in the original
steps.b: Open the pages the AI quoted for deadlines and must-haves and confirm them yourself.
If any must-have is missing or the deadline is too tight, pass and note why so you can spot better tenders next time.

example: Buyer: council seeks a caterer for 12 community events. Deadline: 5pm 14 March (questions by 3 March). Must-haves: £5m public liability, food hygiene rating 4+. Scoring: quality 60%, price 40%. Value: about £18,000. Risk: 30-day payment terms. Fit: 7/10, meets all must-haves but tight staffing in June.
tips: Check the tender's rules on confidentiality before uploading documents to an AI tool.
Insurance and legal requirements are worth confirming with your broker or adviser before you commit.

trigger.detail: Tender documents are added to the Tenders folder

actions.detail: Pull out deadlines, requirements, scoring and value
Score fit and write a bid or no-bid summary
Add the tender deadlines to the calendar

t: Write a clear, welcoming job advert
d: A job ad that explains the role honestly, uses inclusive language, lists only real must-haves and tells people exactly how to apply.
when: Whenever you need to hire

steps.h: Note the facts about the role
steps.b: Write down the job title, hours, pay range, location or remote options, main tasks, and the 3 to 5 skills someone truly needs on day one.

steps.h: Ask AI to draft the advert
steps.b: Paste your notes into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: Write a job advert for a [job title] at [business], a [one-line description]. Facts: [paste notes]. Structure: a 2-line intro on why the role matters, What you'll do (5 bullets), What you'll need (only these must-haves: [list]), Nice to have (max 3), Pay and benefits, How to apply and the closing date. Use plain, inclusive British English: avoid gendered words, age-coded phrases like 'young and dynamic' or 'digital native', and unnecessary requirements like degrees unless essential. Add a line welcoming applicants from all backgrounds and offering adjustments for the application or interview. Keep it under 400 words.

steps.b: Ask the AI: 'List any words or requirements in this ad that might put off women, older people, disabled people or people from other backgrounds, and suggest alternatives.' Then read it yourself, as AI can miss things.

steps.h: Publish and save the final version
steps.b: Save the final ad in Google Docs so it's ready for next time, then post it on your chosen job boards and social channels.

example:
Café Team Member (part-time, 20 hours, £12.60 to £13.50/hour)
What you'll do: make great coffee, keep the counter spotless, chat with regulars...
What you'll need: friendly with customers, reliable on weekend shifts.
No barista experience needed; we'll train you. Tell us if you need any adjustments to apply.
tips: Always include the pay range; it saves everyone time and gets more applications.
Check local employment law, such as minimum wage and right-to-work rules, before you post.

trigger.detail: Manager starts a new vacancy

actions.detail: Draft an inclusive job advert from the role notes
Flag potentially biased words or unnecessary requirements
Save the advert for the manager to review

t: Decide what good looks like before reading CVs
d: A fair scoring sheet with clear criteria and what each score means, agreed before you see any applications, so every candidate is judged the same way.
when: Before the closing date of every vacancy

steps.h: Pick 4 to 6 criteria from the job ad
steps.b: Use the must-haves from your advert, such as 'experience handling customer complaints'. Avoid vague ones like 'good culture fit'.

steps.h: Ask AI to turn them into a rubric
steps.b: Paste your criteria into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: Create a scoring rubric for shortlisting candidates for [job title]. Criteria: [list]. For each criterion, describe what a score of 1 (no evidence), 2 (some evidence), 3 (clear evidence) and 4 (strong, repeated evidence) looks like, with a short example of the kind of evidence that counts. Make sure every criterion relates to the job itself, and point out any that could unfairly disadvantage people because of age, sex, disability, race, religion or other protected characteristics. Format as a table I can paste into a spreadsheet.

steps.b: Paste the rubric into a Google Sheet tab, and make a second tab with a row per candidate, a column per criterion, a total, and a notes column for evidence.

steps.h: Agree it with anyone else involved
steps.b: If others are shortlisting with you, agree the rubric together and score separately before comparing.

example: Criterion: Handling unhappy customers. 1 - no mention. 2 - mentions customer-facing work. 3 - describes resolving a complaint. 4 - several examples, including calming a tense situation and a result. Candidate C-03: 3 (evidence: 'resolved delivery complaints in a busy retail store').
tips: Give candidates a code, like C-01, and score before looking at names, photos or ages where you can.
A person must make every shortlisting decision; the rubric is there to make human judgement more consistent.

trigger.detail: Manager confirms the job's must-have criteria

actions.detail: Create a 1 to 4 scoring rubric for each criterion
Flag criteria that may be unfair or not job-related
Set up the scoring sheet with rubric and candidate rows

t: Check applications against your criteria fairly
d: AI pulls the relevant evidence from each anonymised CV into a table, so you can score every candidate against the same criteria yourself.
when: After the closing date, before shortlisting

steps.b: Check your workplace policy and local law on using AI with candidate data. In the UK and EU, you should tell applicants if AI helps in the process, for example in your privacy notice or job ad.
Save CVs in a private Google Drive folder. Before using AI, give each one a code (C-01, C-02) and remove names, contact details, photos, dates of birth and addresses.

steps.h: Ask AI to find evidence, not to rank
steps.b: Upload or paste a few anonymised CVs at a time with this prompt.
steps.p: I'm shortlisting for [job title]. Criteria: [paste criteria from your rubric]. For each anonymised application below, make a table with one row per criterion: Candidate code, Criterion, Evidence found (quote the exact words from the CV), and 'No evidence found' where relevant. Do not score, rank, or recommend candidates. Do not comment on gaps in employment, age, gender, nationality, schools or anything not in my criteria. Applications: [paste].

steps.b: Use the evidence table alongside the original CV to fill in your scoring sheet. Read each original, because AI can miss or misread things.

steps.h: Check for bias and tidy up
steps.b: Before finalising, look at who you've shortlisted and ask whether anyone was marked down for something unrelated to the job. Delete the AI chats and copies once you're done, in line with your data retention policy.

example:
C-04 | Managing a busy rota | 'Created weekly rotas for a team of 12 across two sites' 
C-04 | Food hygiene | 'Level 2 Food Hygiene certificate (2024)'
C-04 | Supervising staff | No evidence found
C-05 | Managing a busy rota | 'Covered shift planning when manager was on leave'
tips: Candidate data is personal data: use a business AI account with training on your data turned off, and only share what's needed.
Never let AI make or rank the decision; it can repeat hidden biases from its training.

trigger.detail: An anonymised application is added to the shortlisting folder

actions.detail: Quote evidence from the application for each criterion
Add the evidence rows to the scoring sheet
Remind the hiring manager to score and decide in person

t: Prepare fair, structured interview questions
d: A set of the same questions for every candidate, linked to the job's criteria, with follow-up prompts and notes on what a strong answer includes.
when: Before the first interview for a role

steps.b: Use the same criteria as your job ad and scoring sheet, so interviews test the things that matter for the job.

steps.h: Ask AI for the question set
steps.b: Paste this prompt into your AI assistant.
steps.p: Write a structured interview plan for a [job title] at a [type of business]. Criteria: [list]. For each criterion: 1 main question asking for a real example ('Tell me about a time...'), 2 follow-up prompts, and 3 bullet points describing what a strong answer includes. Add 1 practical question or short task suited to the role. Avoid any questions about age, family plans, health, religion, nationality or other personal topics that aren't related to the job, and flag any of my criteria that might lead there. Finish with a 2-minute welcome script and a closing script explaining next steps and timescales. Total interview length: [30/45] minutes.

steps.b: Paste it into Google Docs with space under each question for notes and a score, and use a fresh copy for each candidate.
When you invite candidates, ask whether they need any adjustments, such as extra time, a quiet room or questions in advance.

example:
Criterion: Working under pressure
Q: Tell me about a time several things needed doing at once. What did you do?
Follow-ups: How did you decide what came first? What would you do differently?
Strong answer: prioritises clearly, keeps others informed, reflects on what they learned.
tips: Ask every candidate the same main questions in the same order; it's fairer and makes comparing much easier.
Write notes on what they said, not your impressions of them.

trigger.detail: Interviews are confirmed for a role

actions.detail: Write structured questions and strong-answer guides per criterion
Create an interview pack with scoring space

t: Book interviews without endless email back-and-forth
d: Candidates pick their own interview slot from your calendar and get a clear invitation with everything they need to know.
when: Whenever you invite candidates to interview

steps.b: In Google Calendar, create an appointment schedule for interview slots, if your plan includes it, or use Calendly's free plan. Add a buffer between slots so you can write notes.
Ask your AI assistant to write a friendly, complete invitation.
steps.p: Write an interview invitation email for [job title] at [business]. Include: congratulations on being shortlisted, the interview format ([video on Google Meet / in person at address]), length ([45] minutes), who they'll meet ([names and roles]), what we'll cover, whether there's a task, a link to book a slot [booking link] by [date], a request to tell us about any adjustments they need, and who to contact with questions. Under 180 words, warm and clear, British English.

steps.b: Turn on Templates in Gmail's settings under Advanced, then save the email as a template for this role.
Send the invitation individually or with each candidate in BCC, so no one sees anyone else's email address.

example: Hi [Name], thank you for applying for Bookkeeper at Hartley & Co. We'd love to invite you to a 45-minute video interview with Sarah (Office Manager) and me. We'll talk through your experience and a short spreadsheet exercise. Please book a time here by Friday 12th: [link]. Let us know if you need any adjustments.
tips: Booking pages show your free slots, so check you're only offering times you can really do.
Send a short reminder the day before; it cuts no-shows.

trigger.detail: A candidate is marked Shortlisted in the hiring sheet

actions.detail: Prepare the interview invitation with the booking link
Hold the interview once the candidate books
Remind the candidate the day before

t: Let unsuccessful candidates down kindly
d: Respectful, personal rejection emails for each stage of hiring, with optional feedback that's honest, useful and safe to send.
when: When you've made a hiring decision

steps.h: Write down why, against your criteria
steps.b: For anyone who interviewed, note one or two job-related reasons from your scoring sheet, such as 'less experience of managing budgets than other candidates'.
Paste this prompt into your AI assistant.
steps.p: Write 3 rejection email templates for [job title] at [business]: 1) applied but not shortlisted (under 80 words), 2) interviewed, no detailed feedback (under 100 words), 3) interviewed, with brief feedback (under 140 words) using these points: [job-related points from scoring sheet]. All should thank them sincerely, be clear the decision is final, avoid any comments on personality or anything not related to the job criteria, and wish them well. Template 3 should frame feedback constructively. British English, warm, human. Use [Name] placeholders.

steps.b: Add one specific, genuine line where you can, such as something they did well. Send within a few days of deciding.

example: Hi [Name], thank you for coming in to meet us on Tuesday and for preparing so thoroughly. We enjoyed hearing about your work at the farm shop. We've decided to offer the role to someone with more experience of running stock systems. We'd be happy to hear from you for future roles. Wishing you all the best.
tips: Keep feedback tied to the job criteria; it's fairer and protects you if a decision is ever questioned.
Tell candidates how long you'll keep their details, in line with your privacy notice.

trigger.detail: A candidate's status changes to Unsuccessful

actions.detail: Write a rejection email for the right stage
Save it as a draft for the manager to personalise and send

t: Write up interviews consistently and fairly
d: Turn your interview notes or transcript into a write-up that sets out evidence for each criterion, so the panel can compare candidates on facts.
when: Straight after each interview

steps.b: Only record or use AI note-taking if the candidate agrees, and tell them how long the recording will be kept. If they say no, take written notes; it mustn't affect their chances.
Use Google Meet's 'Take notes for me', Zoom AI Companion or Teams recap if your plan includes it, or type up your handwritten notes. Remove the candidate's name and use their code.

steps.h: Ask AI to organise the evidence
steps.b: Paste the notes into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: Here are notes from an interview for [job title], candidate [code]. Criteria: [list]. Organise the notes into a write-up with one section per criterion: what the candidate said (quote where possible), and gaps or questions to follow up. Do not give a score, recommendation or overall opinion. Do not mention accent, appearance, nervousness, age, family or anything outside the criteria. If notes are unclear, say so. Notes: [paste].

steps.b: Each interviewer scores against the rubric on their own before discussing. Save the write-up in a private Google Doc with restricted sharing.

example:
Candidate C-02, Bookkeeper
Accuracy with figures: 'I reconcile 3 bank accounts weekly and found a £1,200 duplicate payment last year.'
Using Xero: described bank rules and VAT returns. Follow up: no mention of payroll.
Communication: explained a tricky issue to a client clearly.
tips: The hiring decision must be made by people, using the scores and their own judgement, never by an AI.
Interview notes are personal data and candidates can ask to see them, so keep them factual and professional.

trigger.detail: An interview event ends

actions.detail: Organise notes into evidence per criterion without scoring
Save a private write-up for the hiring panel
Remind each interviewer to score separately

t: Send a warm, clear job offer
d: A friendly offer email and a checklist of what the formal offer letter must cover, so your new hire knows exactly what to expect.
when: When you've chosen someone to hire

steps.b: Note the job title, start date, pay, hours, place of work, probation period, holiday, and any conditions such as references or right-to-work checks.
Paste the details into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: Write a job offer email to [first name] for the role of [job title] at [business]. Details: [paste]. Tone: warm and excited but clear. Include: the offer and why we chose them (one genuine line: [reason]), key terms in a short bullet list, conditions of the offer, what happens next and by when, and a request to confirm acceptance by [date]. Under 200 words, British English. Then, separately, give me a checklist of what a written statement of employment terms usually needs to include in [country], so I can check my formal letter or contract covers it.

steps.b: Use the checklist to review your contract or written statement. Have the contract template checked by an HR or employment law professional at least once.
Ring the candidate with the good news, then send the email and formal letter straight after.

example: Hi Tom, I'm delighted to offer you the role of Workshop Technician at Kestrel Bikes. Your mechanical know-how really stood out. Start: Mon 3 March. Pay: £27,500 a year. Hours: 37.5, Tue to Sat. Holiday: 28 days including bank holidays. Subject to two references. Please let me know by Friday 21st.
tips: AI checklists are a starting point, not legal advice; employment rules vary by country.
Keep offer details consistent between the email and the contract to avoid confusion later.

trigger.detail: Manager marks a candidate as Offer

actions.detail: Draft the offer email and terms checklist
Save the offer email for the manager to send after calling
Add a reminder for the acceptance deadline

t: Give every new starter a great first week
d: A day-by-day onboarding plan for a new team member, turned into a Trello board with tasks for you, the starter and their buddy.
when: A week before someone starts

steps.h: Describe the role and your workplace
steps.b: Note what the job involves, who they'll work with, which systems they'll use and anything they must do in week one, such as safety training.
Paste this prompt into your AI assistant.
steps.p: Create an onboarding plan for a new [job title] joining [business], a team of [size]. Role details: [paste]. Give: 1) a before-day-one checklist (equipment, logins, paperwork, welcome message), 2) a day-by-day plan for week 1 with a mix of learning, meeting people and one small real task, 3) goals for the end of week 2, month 1 and month 3, 4) who owns each task: manager, buddy, or new starter. Keep it realistic for a small business and not overloaded. Format as lists I can turn into cards.

steps.b: Create a Trello board with lists for Before day one, Week 1, Month 1 and Month 3. Add each task as a card, assign people and set due dates.
Once it works, use Trello's option to make the board a template or copy it, so each new starter gets the same good experience.

example: Before day one: laptop set up (Manager), send welcome message with first-day details (Manager), pick a lunch spot (Buddy). Day 1: tour, meet the team, set up email. Day 3: shadow two customer calls. Day 5: handle one simple order alone; end-of-week chat. Month 1 goal: running the morning orders.
tips: Add a 'questions so far' card the starter can add to all week; it shows what to explain better next time.
Notion or a shared Google Doc works just as well if your team doesn't use Trello.

trigger.detail: A new starter's start date is 7 days away

actions.detail: Create a tailored onboarding plan for the role
Add onboarding tasks as cards with owners and due dates
Tell the manager and buddy their tasks

t: Run onboarding on autopilot from one form
d: A new-starter form feeds a tracking sheet, sends you an alert, and kicks off scheduled welcome emails and calendar check-ins for every hire.
when: Every time someone accepts a job offer

steps.b: Make a Google Form for the manager to fill in: starter's name, role, start date, manager, buddy, equipment needed. Keep personal details like bank info out of it; collect those through your payroll process.

Link the form to a Google Sheet and turn on email notifications for new responses. Add checklist columns (Contract sent, Equipment ready, Logins set up) with tick boxes, and use conditional formatting to turn a row red if the start date is close and anything is unticked.

steps.h: Write the welcome emails with AI
steps.b: Ask your AI assistant for a set of emails to schedule.
steps.p: Write 3 short emails for new starters at [business]: 1) sent 1 week before starting: warm welcome, first-day time, address, who to ask for, what to bring, dress code, 2) sent the evening before: a friendly 'see you tomorrow' with the plan for day one, 3) sent at the end of week one from the manager: thanks, what's next, and an invitation to share feedback. Each under 120 words, British English, use [brackets] for details. Then list 4 calendar check-ins to book (with timing and a 3-bullet agenda each) for the first 3 months.

steps.b: When a form arrives, fill in the email templates and use Gmail's Schedule send for each one. Create the calendar check-ins with the starter and manager straight away.
Ask each new starter what was missing, and update the form, emails and checklist.

example: New row: Priya S. | Junior Designer | Starts 7 April | Manager: Leon | Buddy: Kat. Contract sent ✓ Equipment ready ✗ (row red: 5 days to go). Scheduled: welcome email 31 March 9am, see-you-tomorrow 6 April 6pm. Check-ins booked: week 1, week 4, week 8, week 12.
tips: Keep the sheet's sharing limited to people who need it, since it holds staff details.
Microsoft Forms, Excel and Outlook can do the same, including scheduled sending in Outlook.

trigger.detail: A manager submits the new-starter form

actions.detail: Add the starter to the onboarding tracker
Schedule the welcome emails at set times before and after the start date
Book the first-week, month-one and month-three check-ins
Alert the manager about unticked tasks close to the start date

t: Write a clear workplace policy in plain English
d: A first draft of a short, readable staff policy, such as remote working or AI use, ready for you to check with an HR professional.
when: When your team needs a rule written down

steps.h: Decide what the policy must say
steps.b: Note what you already do in practice, what problems you want to avoid and any decisions you've made, like core hours or which tools staff may use.

steps.h: Ask AI for a plain-English draft
steps.b: Paste this prompt into your AI assistant.
steps.p: Draft a [topic, e.g. remote working / using AI tools at work / expenses] policy for [business], a [size and type] business in [country]. What we already do and want: [paste notes]. Structure: Purpose (2 lines), Who it applies to, The rules (numbered, plain English), What staff can expect from us, What to do if something goes wrong, Who to ask, and Review date. Under 700 words, friendly but clear, British English. After the draft, list any legal points in [country] I should check with an HR or employment law professional, and any common policy topics I've not covered.

steps.b: Have the draft reviewed by an HR adviser or employment solicitor, especially anything about pay, discipline, data or contracts.
Save the final version in Google Docs, share it with the team and talk it through at a team meeting, inviting questions.

example:
Using AI tools at work
1. You may use approved AI tools (currently ChatGPT Team) for drafting and research.
2. Never paste customer names, contact details or financial information into AI tools.
3. Check AI output before using it; you're responsible for the final work.
Review date: January 2027.
tips: Shorter policies get read; aim for two pages or less.
AI doesn't know current law in your area for certain, so treat the legal checklist as questions for your adviser.

trigger.detail: Manager requests a new policy

actions.detail: Draft a plain-English policy and legal-check list
Save the draft for professional review
Add a review date reminder

t: Answer staff questions from your own handbook
d: A private AI workspace loaded with your staff handbook and policies, so you or your team get quick, accurate answers with the source section named.
when: Whenever someone asks 'what's our policy on...?'

steps.b: Gather your handbook, holiday rules, expenses process and other policies from Google Drive. Make sure none contain individual staff details.
Set up a Project in ChatGPT or Claude, or a Gem in Gemini, and upload the documents. Use a business or team plan if you'll share it with staff, and check your workplace AI policy first.
Paste this into the workspace's instructions.
steps.p: You answer staff questions about policies at [business] using only the uploaded documents. For each answer: give a short, plain-English answer, then name the document and section it comes from. If the documents don't cover the question, say 'This isn't covered in our policies, please ask [name/role]'. Never guess, never give legal advice, and don't comment on individual cases such as someone's pay, performance or health; refer those to [name/role]. British English, friendly.

steps.b: Ask ten questions you get often and check each answer against the handbook before you rely on it.
Replace old files in the workspace the same day a policy changes, and note the date in the instructions.

example: Q: Can I carry over unused holiday? A: Yes, up to 5 days into the next holiday year, which must be used by the end of March. Source: Staff Handbook, section 4.3 'Holiday carry-over'. Q: Can I get a pay rise? A: This isn't covered in our policies, please ask Jo in the office.
tips: Personal issues like sickness, grievances or pay should always go to a person, not an AI.
Keep the handbook itself as the official version; the AI is just a quicker way to find things in it.

trigger.detail: A staff member asks a policy question

actions.detail: Answer from the uploaded handbook and name the section
Pass questions not covered to the named person

t: Prepare for a difficult conversation with a team member
d: A calm plan for a tricky one-to-one, with an opening line, key points, likely reactions and how to agree next steps fairly.
when: Before a performance or behaviour conversation

steps.h: Write down the facts, not the person
steps.b: Note specific examples with dates, the impact on the team or customers, and what you want to change. Use a role instead of the person's name.

steps.h: Ask AI to help you plan
steps.b: Paste this prompt into your AI assistant.
steps.p: Help me prepare for a one-to-one with a [role] about [issue]. Facts: [dated examples and impact]. What I want to happen: [outcome]. Anything I know about their situation: [context, without health details]. Give me: 1) a calm opening of 2 sentences that explains why we're meeting, 2) the 3 key points in plain language, 3) 3 open questions to understand their side, 4) likely reactions (upset, defensive, quiet) and how to respond to each, 5) how to agree clear next steps and a review date, 6) a short summary note I can send afterwards. Supportive but direct, British English. Remind me where I should get HR or legal advice.

steps.b: If the issue could lead to formal action, follow your written disciplinary or performance process and speak to an HR adviser first.

steps.h: Have the conversation and note it
steps.b: Keep your plan in your notes app, have the conversation in private, listen properly, and send the agreed summary afterwards.

example: Opening: 'Thanks for making time. I want to talk about the late starts over the last few weeks and how we can sort it together.' Question: 'Is anything making mornings harder at the moment?' If upset: pause, acknowledge, offer to continue tomorrow. Next step: agree start time, review in 2 weeks.
tips: If someone mentions health, caring duties or personal problems, stop and get HR advice; you may need to make adjustments.
Keep notes factual and store them securely; staff can ask to see what's recorded about them.

trigger.detail: Manager plans a difficult conversation

actions.detail: Create a conversation plan with opening, questions and next steps
Book the follow-up review date

t: Hear what your team really thinks, anonymously
d: A short anonymous pulse survey for your team and an AI summary of themes and suggestions, without anyone being identified.
when: Every three months

steps.b: Ask your AI assistant for a short, balanced survey.
steps.p: Write an anonymous team pulse survey for a [size] person [type of business]. 6 to 8 questions, taking under 5 minutes. Include: 4 rating questions (1 to 5) on workload, support from managers, communication and feeling valued; 2 open questions ('What's one thing we should keep doing?' and 'What's one thing we should change?'); and an optional open comment box. Avoid questions about role, age, location or anything else that could identify people in a small team. Add a 2-line intro explaining it's anonymous and what we'll do with the results.

steps.b: Create the form and set it so names aren't recorded (in Forms, choose that anyone can respond, or turn off recording names). Responses collect in Excel automatically.

steps.h: Share it and give a deadline
steps.b: Send the link to the team in Teams or email with a one-week deadline and a reminder halfway through.
Copy the responses from Excel into your AI assistant and ask for averages, the main themes from comments with counts, and 3 suggested actions. Remove any comment that names someone before pasting.
Tell the team what came up and the one or two changes you'll make. This is what keeps people answering next time.

example: Results (14 of 16 responded): Workload 2.9, Manager support 4.1, Communication 3.2, Feeling valued 3.8. Themes: Friday rush is stressful (7), weekly team huddle helps (6), unclear who covers holidays (4). Actions: publish holiday cover rota; add a Thursday prep slot.
tips: In very small teams, only report results when at least 5 people have answered, so no one can be identified.
Google Forms with Google Sheets works the same way if you don't use Microsoft 365.

trigger.detail: First Monday of each quarter

actions.detail: Send the anonymous survey link to the team
After the deadline, summarise scores and comment themes
Create a results summary for the manager to share

t: Manage holiday requests without clashes or confusion
d: Staff request leave through a form, you see clashes highlighted in a sheet, get an alert, and approved days go straight onto a shared team calendar.
when: Every time someone asks for time off

steps.b: Make a Google Form with: name (dropdown of staff), first day off, last day off, type of leave (holiday, unpaid, other) and an optional note. Turn on email notifications for new responses.

steps.h: Set up the sheet with AI help
steps.b: Link the form to a Google Sheet, then ask your AI assistant for the formulas you need.
steps.p: My Google Sheet of holiday requests has these columns: A Timestamp, B Name, C First day, D Last day, E Leave type, F Note. Give me beginner-friendly, step-by-step instructions to: 1) add column G 'Working days' that counts weekdays between C and D (using NETWORKDAYS), 2) add column H 'Status' with a dropdown of Pending, Approved, Declined, 3) highlight a row orange if its dates overlap with another Approved request, using a custom formula in conditional formatting, 4) make a summary tab showing each person's approved days so far this year against an allowance of [number] days. Give the exact formulas and say where to paste them.

steps.b: Create a separate Google Calendar called Team holidays and share it with staff as view-only.

steps.h: Approve and add to the calendar
steps.b: When an alert arrives, check for orange clashes, set the Status, reply to the person, and add approved leave as an all-day event on the team calendar.
Look at the summary tab once a month and remind anyone who has lots of leave left.

example: New request: Marta | 12 to 16 Aug | Holiday | 5 working days | Pending (orange: overlaps with Dan, Approved 14 to 21 Aug). Summary: Marta 9 of 28 days used; Dan 17 of 28. Team holidays calendar: 'Dan - holiday' 14 to 21 Aug.
tips: Keep 'other' leave notes brief and private; sickness and family reasons are sensitive personal data.
Check that formulas work with a few test requests before you share the form with the team.

trigger.detail: A staff member submits a leave request

actions.detail: Add the request with working days calculated
Check for clashes with approved leave
Alert the manager to approve or decline
Add approved leave to the team holiday calendar

t: Run one-to-ones your team look forward to
d: A simple, repeatable agenda for regular one-to-ones, tailored questions for each person and a short record of what you both agreed.
when: Before each regular one-to-one

steps.b: Set a recurring Google Calendar event, such as 30 minutes every fortnight, with each team member, and attach a shared Google Doc for notes.
Paste this prompt into your AI assistant.
steps.p: Create a 30-minute one-to-one agenda for me (a manager at a [type of business]) and a [role] who has been with us [time]. What I know: recent wins [wins], current challenges [challenges], their goals [goals]. Include: a 5-minute check-in, their topics first, progress on goals, one development question, any feedback both ways, and agreed actions. Suggest 6 open questions I could rotate over the next few months, such as about workload, learning and what support they need. Supportive tone, British English.

steps.b: Paste the agenda into the shared doc a couple of days before and ask them to add what they'd like to talk about at the top.
At the end, write down two or three agreed actions with names and dates in the doc, so you can check them next time.

example: Agenda, 14 May: 1. How are things? (5 min) 2. Ellis's topics: training budget, Friday cover 3. Goal: lead the stock count, on track 4. Question: 'What would make next month easier?' 5. Feedback both ways. Actions: Ellis books first-aid course by 31 May; I sort Friday cover rota.
tips: Keep one-to-ones even when you're busy; cancelling them often sends the wrong message.
Keep notes respectful and factual, as the team member can see them and may ask for them later.
